title: Why Oil Prices Haven't Spiked as Much as Everyone Expected From the Iran War
excerpt: Ghost tanker fleets, bypass pipelines, and demand destruction have kept crude prices well below crisis-level predictions, even as the Strait of Hormuz remains partially blocked.
body:
• Brent crude has fallen from a peak above $126 to around $90, and analysts have cut their 2026 forecasts for the first time since the Iran war began in February.
  • An estimated 2.9 million barrels per day are still flowing through the Strait of Hormuz via toll-paying tankers and "ghost" fleets running with transponders off.
  • Saudi Arabia's 7-million-bpd East-West Pipeline and Abu Dhabi's 1.8-million-bpd bypass pipeline are routing oil around the chokepoint.
  • Demand destruction from higher prices, strategic petroleum reserve releases, and a weakening global economy are absorbing the supply shortfall.

The Price Spike That Didn't Quite Happen

When the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, the oil market braced for catastrophe. The Strait of Hormuz, which had previously carried about 20 million barrels per day — roughly 20% of global crude supply — was effectively shut down. JPMorgan projected supply losses of up to 4.7 million barrels per day. Goldman Sachs, UBS, and ANZ rushed to raise their forecasts. Brent crude surged past $126 a barrel.

Five months later, the strait remains partially blocked, fighting has erupted in Lebanon, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards have stopped tankers and fired warning shots at commercial vessels. Yet Brent has dropped back to roughly $90. WTI briefly touched pre-war levels in June before rebounding. Analysts are cutting their forecasts, not raising them.

The market, as SEB Research analyst Ole Hvalbye put it, "has stopped trading the war and started trading the shipping data."

The Ghost Fleet Factor

Visible tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is running at about 15% of pre-war levels, according to JPMorgan estimates based on Kpler ship-tracking data. That number suggests a massive supply gap. But the actual shortfall is smaller than it appears.

Piper Sandler estimates that around 2.9 million barrels per day made it through the strait last month. About 2.1 million came from tankers that paid tolls to Iran — Tehran has imposed a "maritime service fee" on vessels transiting the waterway. Another 900,000 barrels per day moved through via "ghost" transits: tankers running at night with their transponders switched off, slipping past Iranian naval patrols in the dark.

"Prices are not falling because the market suddenly believes the geopolitical risk has vanished. They are falling because the physical-flow picture is improving faster than expected."

— Stephen Innes, Managing Partner, SPI Asset Management

Bypass Pipelines Absorb the Pressure

Two major pipeline systems are routing oil around the chokepoint entirely. Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, with a capacity of 7 million barrels per day, connects the kingdom's eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the strait completely. Abu Dhabi's 1.8-million-bpd pipeline does the same, connecting Habshan to the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.

These pipelines existed before the war but operated well below capacity. With the strait disrupted, they are running at or near full throughput. The combined 8.8 million bpd of bypass capacity has prevented the kind of total supply shock that early worst-case scenarios envisioned.

Demand Destruction and Reserve Drawdowns

Higher oil prices have also curbed demand. When Brent crossed $100, consumers and businesses began cutting back on fuel consumption. Airlines reduced flight frequencies. Shipping companies rerouted vessels around Africa rather than paying Iranian tolls. Industrial demand in China and Europe softened as energy costs ate into margins.

Governments have also tapped strategic reserves. The U.S. released barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to stabilize domestic gasoline prices, though the reserve is now at historically low levels. Other IEA member nations have coordinated smaller releases.

What Analysts Expect Next

A Reuters poll of 31 economists and analysts projects Brent will average $84.50 per barrel in 2026, down from $90.44 projected a month earlier — the first downward revision since the war began. Brent is expected to ease to around $79 by Q4 2026 and settle in the mid-$70s by mid-2027.

The key variable remains the Strait of Hormuz. A U.S.-Iran peace deal signed in June included provisions for the strait's full reopening, but implementation has been halting. A limited number of vessels pass through daily under coordination with Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy. Whether traffic normalizes depends on unresolved questions: toll structures, routing security, and whether Iran's proposed navigation-fee framework survives the agreement.

"If traffic through the Strait of Hormuz comes back to normal, we will go back to supply surplus on the oil markets," LBBW's head of commodity research Frank Schallenberger told Reuters. "Therefore prices will continue to go down in the second half of 2026."

For now, the market is pricing in a messy middle: neither full blockade nor full reopening, with workarounds keeping just enough oil flowing to prevent a supply crisis.
